passage: By eight every evening, the fifth floor of the startup was mostly empty, apart from the interns. Pallavi glanced at Uday's screen: he was still on the slides for a review that was not his job. "Send me the last three; I'll finish the charts," she said. Tomorrow he would do the same for her. They also traded tips: which meeting rooms were quiet, which senior answered questions patiently, how to say no to a Sunday call. On Friday Uday said, "All of us are working past eight. Maybe we should say so." They wrote a short, polite note together, with six names on it, asking about working hours and stipend timing. The manager read it twice. "Let's talk on Monday," she said. Pallavi's knees felt shaky, but she wasn't alone.

qa.q: What time was the fifth floor mostly empty every evening?
qa.a: It was mostly empty by eight every evening, apart from the interns.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi's knees feel shaky when the manager said "Let's talk on Monday"?
qa.a: She was nervous about how the manager might react to a complaint, but she felt steadier because six interns had signed together.

qa.q: What could the interns do before Monday's meeting?
qa.a: They can agree on the points they will raise, such as hours and stipend timing, keep their tone polite, and keep supporting each other instead of competing.

qa.q: How might the manager see the interns' note?
qa.a: The manager read it twice, so it clearly got attention. Six names suggest a shared concern rather than one person's grumble, and the reply was to invite a talk.

grounding: Interns cover for each other, share tips and together raise concerns about hours and pay.
